eligibility_reason: Computational reproduction of Izhikevich (2006): the authors re-implement the polychronization network in NEST (bitwise-identical and independent 'qualitative' versions), run it with many new random seeds, and compare network dynamics and polychronous-group counts with the original's reported findings, then test robustness via 'generalizing reproductions'. Eligibility is itself debatable (simulation study / reproducibility guide rather than an empirical replication with participants).

effects.replication_study: Section 3.2 identical (bitwise) NEST reproduction, 100 runs with different random seeds
effects.outcome: Network activity of the STDP spiking network: slow oscillations and gamma rhythm (power-spectrum gamma peak), bimodal weight distribution
effects.contrast: not applicable: descriptive model behavior compared with the original's reported dynamics
effects.timepoint: final 10 s of an 18,000 s simulation
effects.description: Izhikevich (2006) reported that a minimal network of randomly coupled Izhikevich neurons with STDP and axonal delays self-organizes into activity with slow oscillations and gamma rhythms.
effects.citation_sentence: As we believe that concrete illustrations are necessary to convincingly motivate recommendations, we provide these by reproducing a seminal study in computational neuroscience, a minimal network generating polychronous groups (Izhikevich, 2006).
effects.evidence: Section 3.2.2: 'the NEST simulation yielded identical results to the original version over the entire 18,000 s simulation period.' and 'In the majority of cases (87%), the network activity results in a power spectrum with a high gamma peak around 60 Hz ... However, the rest of the simulation runs result in a lower peak at 40Hz, an eventuality not reported in the original study.'
effects.notes: Bitwise reproduction matches the original C++ code exactly; gamma dynamics reproduced in all runs, but 13% of seeds show an unreported low-gamma (40 Hz) mode. Coded success because the reported gamma dynamics appear; a coder could call it inconclusive given the second mode. The authors' first NEST iteration (3.2.1) failed ('Our first iteration fails to reproduce the key findings of the original study') but was a debugging step superseded by the final iteration, so no separate row. Section 3.1 (re-running the author's own C++ code: 'successfully replicates the main results reported in that study', 4,305 groups, gamma rhythms) is treated as a computational reproducibility check of the original code rather than a replication entry; both candidate coders built their single success row largely on that sentence, and a second coder might add it as a direct success row. Whether simulation reproductions count as 'new data' at all is the main eligibility doubt.

effects.replication_study: Section 3.2 identical (bitwise) NEST reproduction, 100 runs with different random seeds
effects.outcome: Number of polychronous groups that emerge in the network (original reported 5,000-6,000), found by the original group-finding algorithm
effects.contrast: not applicable: group count compared with the original's reported number
effects.description: Izhikevich (2006) reported that the STDP network spontaneously forms a large number (about 5,000-6,000) of polychronous groups, i.e., time-locked but not synchronous firing patterns.
effects.citation_sentence: The polychronization network model was proposed by Izhikevich (2006) as a minimal spiking neural network model capable of exhibiting polychronization, consisting of randomly coupled point neurons expressing STDP (see Section 2.1 for a detailed network description).
effects.evidence: Section 3.2.2: 'For the high gamma state, the mean number of groups detected was 2, 500 ... For the 13 low gamma runs, a mean of 1, 600 groups ... Notably, both distributions are lower than the figure of 5, 000−6, 000 reported in the original study.'
effects.notes: Thousands of polychronous groups emerge, as claimed, but consistently fewer than the 5,000-6,000 reported, and the count depends on the dynamical state. The authors do not call this a success or failure. Coded inconclusive (qualitative claim reproduced, quantitative claim not); success or failure are both defensible readings. Both candidates coded the paper's overall replication as success; kept inconclusive because Section 3.2.2's group counts fall below the original's.

effects.replication_study: Section 3.3 qualitative reproduction (independent NEST implementation with its own randomness and standard synapse numerics), 100 seeds
effects.outcome: Network activity: firing rates, gamma-band power-spectrum peak, final weight distribution
effects.contrast: not applicable: descriptive model behavior compared with the original
effects.timepoint: final 10 s of an 18,000 s simulation
effects.description: Izhikevich (2006) reported that a minimal network of randomly coupled Izhikevich neurons with STDP and axonal delays self-organizes into activity with slow oscillations and gamma rhythms.
effects.citation_sentence: We therefore developed a network model that reproduces the original in the commonly understood sense, i.e., all concepts of the original are faithfully translated into the new framework.
effects.evidence: Section 3.3: 'Figures 6, 7 demonstrates that the qualitative reproduction captures the key features of the original model. The raster plots are visually similar ... the power spectra (Figure 6C) to those of the original model. Likewise, the final weight distributions (Figure 6B) overlap almost completely.' But: 'the proportion of high gamma and low gamma states have reversed (14 high gamma simulations, 86 low gamma simulations)'.
effects.notes: The authors' explicit statement ('captures the key features of the original model') supports success. However, 86% of seeds converge to the low-gamma (40 Hz) state, not the high-gamma (~60 Hz) state the original showed, so inconclusive is a plausible alternative. Type: same paradigm re-implemented in a different simulator with standard numerics and its own random streams (methodology changed, context same), so close experiment; direct is also defensible.

effects.replication_study: Section 3.3 qualitative reproduction (independent NEST implementation), 100 seeds
effects.outcome: Number of polychronous groups that emerge (original reported 5,000-6,000)
effects.contrast: not applicable: group count compared with the original's reported number
effects.description: Izhikevich (2006) reported that the STDP network spontaneously forms a large number (about 5,000-6,000) of polychronous groups, i.e., time-locked but not synchronous firing patterns.
effects.citation_sentence: We therefore developed a network model that reproduces the original in the commonly understood sense, i.e., all concepts of the original are faithfully translated into the new framework.
effects.evidence: Section 3.3: 'In line with the bitwise reproduction, simulations exhibiting a high gamma peak yield more groups than the simulations exhibiting a low gamma peak (median 2, 700, IQR 1,300 vs. median 1, 500 IQR: 800; Figure 7C).'
effects.notes: Groups emerge in the thousands, but below the original's 5,000-6,000, and most runs are in the low-gamma state with about 1,500 groups. The authors say the reproduction 'captures the key features' without addressing the group count against the original. Coded inconclusive; success is a plausible alternative reading.

effects.replication_study: Section 3.4 generalizing reproductions (qualitative model with Poisson stimulus, modified plasticity, uniform/shorter delays, finer integration and 0.1 ms resolution; 10 seeds each)
effects.outcome: Number of polychronous groups the network forms, under comparable network dynamics
effects.contrast: original configuration vs biologically/numerically relaxed configurations
effects.description: Izhikevich (2006) reported that a spiking network with STDP and axonal conduction delays generically self-organizes into a large number of polychronous groups.
effects.citation_sentence: Beyond the practical steps that can be taken to improve the quality of model code and related artifacts, in the course of our study we have identified several unusual assumptions and numerics choices in the original simulation and analysis code, and investigated to what extent the reported model behavior depends on them (sections 3.4, 3.5).
effects.evidence: Section 4 Discussion: 'Thus we conclude that the main reported results of the original study generalize very poorly.' and 'in a network running at a higher resolution of 0.1ms, we found a massive reduction of groups ... it demonstrates that the majority of the polychronous groups reported in the original study can be attributed to artificial synchrony brought about by an unsuitable choice of numerics (low resolution).' Section 3.4.4: 'the original study significantly overstates the number of groups to be found in such networks'.
effects.notes: These are robustness tests of a model, not repetitions of the original set-up; the authors call them 'generalizing reproductions'. Group counts swing by orders of magnitude in both directions: about 90% fewer with a Poisson stimulus, 151 at 0.1 ms resolution, and far more with some plasticity or delay changes. The no-additive-value variant is unchanged. Failure follows the authors' explicit conclusion. Some coders may treat this section as sensitivity analysis rather than a replication and give it no row (neither candidate coded it). Close extension because the paradigm is preserved while the model conditions are deliberately varied to test generality; conceptual is a possible alternative.

effects.replication_study: Section 3.4 generalizing reproductions (delay-distribution changes; 'locked' and 0.1 ms high-resolution integration configurations)
effects.contrast: original 1 ms integration and structured delays vs higher-resolution integration and altered delay distributions
effects.description: Izhikevich (2006) reported that the network spontaneously exhibits gamma-band rhythms (interpreted as a 'wake'/cognitive state) alongside slow 'sleep-like' oscillations.
effects.citation_sentence: We thus conclude that the choice of delay range beyond that found within a local cortical area is critical for the model behavior, and as such should be clearly reported.
effects.evidence: Section 3.4.4: 'The spectral peak is found at around 40Hz for the original, but around 25Hz for the locked and high resolution configurations. We thus conclude that the gamma band oscillation is an artifact of the low resolution of the integration step.' Section 3.4.3: 'In all cases the gamma oscillations are lost, meaning (in Izhikevich's interpretation) that the network model stays "sleeping" and never "wakes up."'
effects.notes: The citation sentence does not itself name Izhikevich (2006) with a year; the section's attribution is 'Izhikevich (2006) argues that this very wide distribution is biologically motivated' (3.4.3). Whether a robustness probe of a secondary dynamical claim should be a row at all is debatable. Some plasticity variants were 'exclusively in the high gamma state', so the gamma loss is specific to the delay and resolution changes, but the authors' conclusion is unambiguous ('artifact').

effects.replication_study: Section 3.5 surrogate analysis on realizations of the bitwise-identical reproduction
effects.outcome: Number of polychronous groups in STDP-grown networks vs networks with randomly assigned strong synapses
effects.contrast: grown (activity-dependent) connectivity vs random surrogate connectivity with matched proportion of strong synapses
effects.timepoint: not applicable: analysis of final connectivity
effects.description: Izhikevich (2006) reported that networks whose strong synapses developed through STDP contain more polychronous groups than shuffled/random networks with the same synapses.
effects.citation_sentence: The original C++ code provides a similar functionality, by shuffling the excitatory-excitatory connections.
effects.evidence: Section 3.5: 'In line with the original findings, networks with randomly selected strong excitatory-excitatory synapses exhibit fewer groups ... than those where the strong synapses develop due to network activity. ... However, if the strong synapses are randomly selected from all excitatory synapses, the opposite tendency is found ... Hence, the algorithm finds either more or fewer groups in grown networks than random networks, depending on what assumption is used to generate the latter.'
effects.notes: The finding is reproduced under the original's surrogate assumption (excitatory-excitatory only) and reversed under the authors' alternative surrogate, so it is coded inconclusive (it holds only under one of two null models). The citation sentence refers to the original only implicitly ('the original C++ code'). The surrogate procedure differs from the original's shuffling, so the type is close experiment. A coder could also skip this row, treating it as a critique of the analysis rather than a replication of a claim. The original's claim that about 90% of stable groups are found active in the spiking (3.5) was not tested ('we were not able to confirm this relationship'), so it gets no row.
